name: std::atomic counter increment versus std::mutex-guarded counter
listed_description: Incrementing a shared counter with a std::atomic integer instead of locking a std::mutex around a plain integer; the book times both, plus a naive atomic_flag spinlock, in Chapter 5.
listed_license: MIT (repository license shown on the GitHub page; the book itself states none)
claim_text: Table 5.1: each thread adds 1 to a counter 200 million times; atomic counter 0.82 s, 4.52 s and 9.13 s versus mutex 1.03 s, 10.15 s and 24.61 s at one, two and four threads.
book_benchmark: Counter incremented 200 million times per thread, with 1, 2 and 4 threads. Compared std::mutex, a simple spinlock (slower than the mutex, 1.33 s, 39.14 s, 128.84 s) and std::atomic counter. Compiler, flags and CPU are not stated in the chunk. The book says both mutex and atomic variants could be tuned further; the code is in the companion repo for readers to rerun.
found_in: book: Asynchronous Programming with C++ (2024), ch. 5, section Example - simple spin-lock implemented using the C++ atomic flag, subsection Simple spin lock issues (Table 5.1)

name: Book SPSC lock-free bounded queue (atomics, power-of-two ring buffer)
listed_description: Single-producer single-consumer bounded queue built on a std::vector ring buffer with std::atomic head and tail indices and acquire-release ordering, as the lock-free counterpart of the mutex and condition-variable queue from Chapter 4. Source file Chapter_05/5x09-SPSC_lock_free_queue.cpp.
listed_license: MIT (repository license shown on the GitHub page; the book itself states none)
book_benchmark: No timings in this chunk. The book says this version performs adequately and defers measurement and optimisation (false sharing, true sharing) to Chapter 13, which is outside this chunk; a later chunk may carry the numbers.
guessed_baseline: mutex plus condition_variable synchronized queue from Chapter 4
found_in: book: Asynchronous Programming with C++ (2024), ch. 5, section SPSC lock-free queue (Chapter 13 revisits performance)

name: Power-of-two ring buffer index masking instead of modulo
listed_description: Wrap queue indices with a bitwise AND against size minus one, using power-of-two capacity, to avoid the division instruction behind the modulo operator.
listed_license: MIT (repository license shown on the GitHub page; the book itself states none)
claim_text: Modulo needs a division instruction, which is expensive; masking with a power-of-two size is much faster (no numbers given).
book_benchmark: None; qualitative claim only, with no timing, compiler or CPU stated in this chunk.
guessed_baseline: ring buffer index wrap using the % operator
found_in: book: Asynchronous Programming with C++ (2024), ch. 5, section SPSC lock-free queue, subsection Why do we use a power of 2 buffer size?
